title: Drift, Gene Flow and Competing Explanations

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Populations started at the same allele frequency and kept alike, so that chance shows up as a spread among them, are called {{c1::replicate populations}}.
cards.quote: The key tool is replicate populations: populations started at the same allele frequency and kept alike, so chance shows up as a spread among them.

cards.front: Across replicate populations, how does the signature of genetic drift differ from that of gene flow or consistent selection?
cards.back: Drift spreads the replicates' allele frequencies apart without pushing their average. Gene flow and consistent selection push the average.
cards.quote: Across replicate populations, drift spreads allele frequencies apart without pushing their average; gene flow and consistent selection push the average.

cards.front: What three kinds of evidence separate drift, selection and gene flow as causes of an allele-frequency change?
cards.back: Compare the replicates' average with a neutral null (what chance alone predicts); test selection with an independent fitness assay; test gene flow with measures of immigration and ancestry.
cards.quote: compare the replicates' average with a neutral null (what chance alone predicts), then test selection with an independent fitness assay and gene flow with measures of immigration and ancestry.

cards.front: Why can the allele-frequency change in one population, on its own, not tell drift from selection?
cards.back: One population gives a single draw from drift's scatter, so luck and cause look the same. The forces are told apart by the spread versus the average across replicates.
cards.quote: One population's frequency, on its own, cannot tell luck from cause, and an unchanged average does not exclude selection (Going deeper).

cards.front: What is genetic drift, and which two chance steps in a real population produce it?
cards.back: Chance change in allele frequency. It comes from which of a parent's two copies goes into each egg or sperm, and how many offspring each parent leaves.
cards.quote: which of a parent's two copies goes into each egg or sperm, and how many offspring each parent leaves

cards.front: A harmful allele rises in frequency over several generations in a small, isolated population. Must selection be the cause?
cards.back: No. Drift needs no fitness difference and acts on all alleles alike, so it can carry a harmful allele up, especially in small populations.
cards.why: Selection would need evidence beyond one population: replicates and a fitness assay.
cards.quote: so it acts on all alleles alike and can carry a harmful allele up or a beneficial one to loss, especially in small populations

cards.front: In the Wright-Fisher model, why does drift's scatter in allele frequency shrink as the population grows?
cards.back: Each generation's 2N gene copies are a random sample of the parents' pool, and a bigger sample is a closer copy of that pool.
cards.quote: A bigger sample is a closer copy of the pool, so the scatter shrinks as 2N grows

cards.front: In a closed neutral population, an allele's chance of fixing (reaching frequency 1) equals its {{c1::current frequency}}.
cards.quote: So a neutral allele's chance of fixing, reaching frequency 1, equals its current frequency

cards.front: Why does a neutral allele's chance of fixing equal its current frequency?
cards.back: Far enough ahead, every copy of the gene descends from one copy alive now. Under neutrality that ancestor is a random pick, so it carries the allele with probability equal to the allele's frequency.
cards.quote: Under neutrality that ancestor is a random pick, and 60% of today's copies carry this allele.

cards.front: A neutral allele is at frequency 0.25 in a closed population that drifts until one allele is left. What is the probability that this allele is lost?
cards.back: 0.75. Fixation probability = current frequency = 0.25, so loss probability = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75.
cards.quote: at 0.60 it is lost 40% of the time

cards.front: The size of the ideal population that drifts as fast as a real one, usually below the census size N, is the {{c1::effective population size (Ne)}}.
cards.quote: So drift is scaled by the effective population size (Ne), the size of the ideal population that drifts as fast, usually below N.

cards.front: Give three reasons a real population drifts faster than its census size N suggests.
cards.back: A few parents leave most of the offspring, so the next generation samples only those few; an uneven breeding sex ratio; and a size that swings from year to year.
cards.quote: if a few parents leave most of the offspring, the next generation samples only those few

cards.front: A sharp drop in numbers that leaves a chance sample of the original gene pool is a {{c1::bottleneck}}.
cards.quote: A bottleneck is a sharp drop in numbers that leaves a chance sample of the original gene pool.

cards.front: What is a founder effect?
cards.back: A new population starts from a few individuals who carry an unrepresentative sample of their source population's variation.
cards.quote: A founder effect occurs when a new population starts from a few individuals who carry an unrepresentative sample of their source population's variation.

cards.front: A resident population has allele frequency 0.50. After migration, immigrants with frequency 0.90 make up m = 0.20 of the breeding pool. What is the frequency after mixing, and how big is the shift?
cards.back: Weighted average: p = 0.80 x 0.50 + 0.20 x 0.90 = 0.40 + 0.18 = 0.58. Shift = +0.08, deterministic (the same every time).
cards.quote: The mixed frequency is a weighted average: p = 0.90 x 0.60 + 0.10 x 0.20 = 0.54 + 0.02 = 0.56.

cards.front: A neutral allele is at 0.20. The next generation is 200 diploid offspring (2N = 400 copies). What standard deviation in allele frequency does one generation of drift produce?
cards.back: Variance = p(1 - p)/2N = 0.20 x 0.80 / 400 = 0.0004. SD = square root = 0.02, about 2 percentage points.

cards.front: In a neutral sampling model, the number of gene copies sampled each generation is cut 100-fold. How much larger does the scatter from drift get?
cards.back: The variance grows 100-fold, but the standard deviation (the scatter in frequency units) grows only by the square root of 100: 10 times.
cards.quote: No, about three times (the square root of 10 is 3.16).

cards.front: After migration shifts a frequency to 0.56, the next generation is sampled by neutral drift. What does migration contribute, and what does drift contribute?
cards.back: Migration gives a deterministic shift, the same every time. Drift adds no push: the expected frequency stays 0.56, with only random scatter around it.
cards.quote: Gene flow shifted the frequency by 0.56 - 0.60 = -0.04, a deterministic shift, the same every time.

cards.front: Buri's Drosophila lines had 16 breeding flies each but drifted as fast as an ideal population of about 9. What did Buri think explained the gap?
cards.back: He said the cause was not known, but judged that variation in how many offspring each fly left, down to complete sterility, was certainly part of it; crowding for egg-laying space probably played a role.
cards.quote: variation in how many offspring each fly left, down to complete sterility, was certainly part of it
cards.section: Buri's 107 fly lines: drift as a distribution

cards.front: Buri's 107 fly lines spread apart in allele frequency, and the changes matched what sampling alone predicts, with no evidence of selection. What may you conclude?
cards.back: The pattern is consistent with drift, not proof of it. Matching a neutral null fails to reject chance; it does not exclude every other cause.
cards.quote: The pattern is consistent with drift rather than proof of it
cards.section: Buri's 107 fly lines: drift as a distribution

cards.front: One random male-female pair of brown anoles from a single source was released on each of seven small islands, all with narrower perches than the source. What two results appeared, and what does each show?
cards.back: Genetic and body differences that tracked the founding pairs persisted (the spread: drift from founders). All populations evolved shorter hindlimbs (a shared shift in the average: selection).
cards.quote: And all the populations evolved shorter hindlimbs, the direction predicted for lizards on narrow perches: a shared shift in the average, the pattern selection predicts.
cards.section: Founders and frontiers: anoles on islands, bacteria on agar

cards.front: Two E. coli strains differing only in a fluorescent label are mixed and the colony spreads across agar. It breaks into single-colour sectors. Why, given the huge number of cells?
cards.back: Chance in the thin band of pioneer cells at the edge decides which colour is carried outward. A spreading front is a series of founder events; the head count is not what chance acts on.
cards.quote: because chance in the thin band of pioneer cells at the edge decided which colour got carried outward
cards.section: Founders and frontiers: anoles on islands, bacteria on agar

cards.front: The movement of alleles between populations by individuals or gametes, pollen included, is {{c1::gene flow}}.
cards.quote: Gene flow is the movement of alleles between populations by individuals or gametes, pollen included.

cards.front: Two populations at allele frequencies 0.20 and 0.80 each receive immigrants with frequency p_m = 0.40, at m = 0.25. Using a change of m x (p_m - p), find each new frequency and the new gap.
cards.back: 0.20 + 0.25 x 0.20 = 0.25; 0.80 + 0.25 x (-0.40) = 0.70. The gap shrinks from 0.60 to 0.45: populations that drifted apart move by different amounts.
cards.quote: populations that had drifted apart move by different amounts, and the gap shrinks from 0.40 to 0.36

cards.front: A drop in a population's mean fitness caused by immigrant alleles that suit somewhere else is {{c1::migration load}}.
cards.quote: Migration load is a drop in a population's mean fitness caused by immigrant alleles that suit somewhere else.

cards.front: Across 25 natural Timema walking-stick populations, those receiving more immigrants from the other host plant were more poorly camouflaged. How strong is this as evidence for migration load, and why?
cards.back: It fits the migration-load prediction but is a correlation across natural populations, not a manipulation of migration, so it cannot by itself show cause.
cards.quote: It is a correlation that fits the migration-load prediction, not a manipulation of migration.

cards.front: A rise in a small population's fitness or growth caused by the genetic effects of gene flow, not just by extra bodies, is {{c1::genetic rescue}}.
cards.back: Extra bodies alone would be demographic rescue.
cards.quote: That makes this genetic rescue: a rise in a small population's fitness or growth caused by the genetic effects of gene flow

cards.front: Two small, isolated Trinidadian guppy populations began receiving immigrants and were followed with pedigrees. What happened, and what pointed to a genetic rather than a demographic cause?
cards.back: Both populations grew nearly tenfold. On average hybrids lived longer and reproduced more than residents or immigrants; the fit hybrids point to a genetic cause.
cards.quote: Both populations grew nearly tenfold, and on average hybrids lived longer and reproduced more than residents or immigrants

cards.front: The movement of alleles from one species into another through hybridization followed by backcrossing is {{c1::introgression}}.
cards.quote: introgression is the movement of alleles from one species into another through hybridization followed by backcrossing

cards.front: Gulf killifish in polluted Texas water carry tolerance-associated variants inferred to come from Atlantic killifish. What roles did gene flow and selection each play?
cards.back: Gene flow (introgression from Atlantic killifish) supplied the variation; strong selection in the polluted water then raised its frequency.
cards.quote: gene flow supplied the variation, and strong selection raised it

cards.front: Gene flow lowered fitness in Timema walking-sticks but raised it in Trinidadian guppies. What decides which way it goes?
cards.back: What the incoming alleles do in their new home: alleles suited elsewhere cause migration load; useful variation can rescue a small population.
cards.quote: Whether gene flow harms or helps depends on what the incoming alleles do in their new home.

cards.front: Ten replicate populations start at the same frequency in the same setting. Each scatters, but their average moves steadily toward allele A, and no immigrants arrive. Which explanation fits, and what fitness-assay result would support it?
cards.back: Consistent selection favouring A. In an independent fitness assay, the favoured genotypes should do better.
cards.why: Drift spreads replicates without pushing the average; with gene flow excluded, a pushed average points to selection.
cards.quote: Drift spreads replicates without pushing their average; gene flow and consistent selection push it.

cards.front: If selection favours a recessive allele, which genotypes should do better in a fitness assay?
cards.back: Only its homozygotes; heterozygotes carry the allele but do not show its advantage.
cards.quote: The favoured genotypes do better (for a recessive allele, only its homozygotes)

cards.front: In expanding bacterial colonies, one fluorescent strain forms large sectors. Design an experiment to tell whether it is fitter or got lucky at the frontier.
cards.back: Grow many replicate colonies from one mix (say 20 at 50:50) and compare the mean fraction with a calibrated neutral model. Swap the labels and repeat. Measure each strain's expansion speed alone.
cards.why: Replicates separate scatter from a shifted mean; the label swap removes a marker cost; solo growth is a fitness assay independent of the sectors.
cards.quote: swap the fluorescent labels and repeat, so any cost of carrying a marker shows up

cards.front: Twenty colonies start at 50:50 of strains X and Y. Strain X averages 0.72 of each colony, well beyond a calibrated neutral model, and still averages about 0.72 after the fluorescent labels are swapped. What does this indicate?
cards.back: Evidence of selection favouring strain X on agar. The mean shift exceeds the neutral null, and because it follows the strain rather than the label, a marker cost does not explain it; an independent expansion-speed assay would confirm it.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that drift scatters replicates but does not shift their mean.
cards.quote: a consistent shift in the mean fraction, beyond what a neutral model calibrated to your colonies allows, is evidence of selection

cards.front: A bacterial strain consistently outgrows another on agar plates. Can you conclude it is fitter in general, for example in well-mixed liquid culture?
cards.back: No. Some strains rank differently on agar than in well-mixed liquid, so the result holds only for the plate.
cards.quote: A strain that wins on a plate has been shown to win on a plate.

cards.front: List the assumptions of the Wright-Fisher model.
cards.back: A closed population of N diploid individuals, constant size, non-overlapping generations, random mating, and no selection, mutation or migration.
cards.why: Real populations break these, which is why Ne differs from N.
cards.quote: A closed population of N diploid individuals, constant in size, with non-overlapping generations, random mating, no selection, no mutation and no migration.

cards.front: In a neutral model with no mutation or migration, what happens to expected heterozygosity over generations, and what can restore it?
cards.back: It falls each generation, faster when Ne is small. Gene flow can restore it; mutation and balancing selection can maintain it.
cards.quote: So small, isolated populations lose variation, which gene flow can restore.

cards.front: What rough rule says whether drift or selection dominates the fate of an allele?
cards.back: Compare Ne x s (s = proportional fitness advantage or cost). Well below 1: drift dominates. Well above 1: selection does. The value 1 is not a sharp crossover.
cards.quote: when Ne multiplied by the selection coefficient s (an allele's proportional fitness advantage or cost) is well below 1, drift dominates

cards.front: An allele has s = 0.001. Using the Ne x s rule, which force dominates when Ne = 50, and when Ne = 10,000?
cards.back: Ne = 50: Ne x s = 0.05, well below 1, so drift dominates. Ne = 10,000: Ne x s = 10, well above 1, so selection does.
cards.quote: when it is well above 1, selection does

cards.front: A population counts 10,000 adults, but nearly all offspring come from a few breeders, giving Ne of about 100. An allele has s = 0.001. Does selection or drift dominate its fate?
cards.back: Drift. Ne x s = 100 x 0.001 = 0.1, well below 1. N x s would be 10, but drift is scaled by Ne, not the head count.
cards.why: Combines the Ne below N rule with the Ne x s rule.
cards.quote: Real populations drift faster than their census size N, the head count, suggests

cards.front: Replicate populations keep their average allele frequency at the starting value, but their spread is much narrower than a neutral model predicts. What explanation fits?
cards.back: Balancing selection, such as heterozygote advantage with its balance point at the starting frequency. It holds the average still while restraining drift's spread.
cards.why: An unchanged average does not exclude selection; the spread must also be compared with the neutral null.
cards.quote: can hold the replicate average still while keeping the spread narrower than drift alone would
cards.section: Selection that leaves the average alone

cards.front: A small, isolated population has lost much heterozygosity and its growth is poor. Managers plan to bring in immigrants. Predict when this should help and when it could harm.
cards.back: It should help if incoming alleles do well in the new home, restoring variation and possibly giving genetic rescue as in the guppies. It could harm if they suit somewhere else, causing migration load as in Timema.
cards.why: Rests on: gene flow restores lost variation, and its effect depends on what incoming alleles do in their new home.
cards.quote: Nor did the immigrants simply replace the residents: alleles putatively associated with local adaptation were not entirely swamped.
